analyses.title: Bridging the gap between tracking and detecting changes on XML
analyses.research_question: Can an XML differencing algorithm be designed for text-centric documents so that its detected changes more closely resemble human-oriented change tracking while retaining acceptable computational performance?
analyses.methodology: The authors develop JNDiff, a Java XML differencing system that linearizes DOM trees into virtual-tree sequences, identifies large matching regions, and then refines unmatched or partially matched regions into insertions, deletions, updates, moves, and expanded matches. They evaluate output quality against XyDiff and faxma using five manually or change-tracking-derived gold-standard document pairs and a human-oriented scoring function based on edit count, affected nodes, and affected characters. They additionally construct a synthetic corpus from 60 XML documents in several text-centric formats, generate versions with varying change ratios, and compare edit-script or delta size and execution time across multiple XML differencing tools.

key_findings.finding: JNDiff obtained the highest aggregate human-oriented quality scores among the evaluated systems on the five document-level quality tests.
On the detailed DL2221 case containing 14 gold-standard changes, JNDiff's aggregate quality score was 25.199, compared with 12.833 for faxma and 13.545 for XyDiff.

The synthetic evaluation starts from 60 heterogeneous XML files and produces 480 files spanning multiple document formats and change ratios, providing broader stress testing than the small manually inspected set.
JNDiff generally produces compact descriptions of changes on text-centric XML and avoids many structurally verbose edits generated by algorithms optimized for data-centric XML.

JNDiff trades execution speed for change-description quality: faxma is faster, JNDiff averaged about 1.1 seconds on the real-document sample, and all evaluated algorithms averaged below two seconds on the synthetic collection.
The method does not establish stable element identities across an arbitrary sequence of document revisions; it computes pairwise correspondence and edit operations between two XML versions.

limitations: The implementation uses DOM trees, so memory consumption constrains processing of very large XML files.
Worst-case matching complexity remains quadratic in the node counts of the two input documents.
JNDiff is deliberately optimized for text-centric XML and is slower than several data-oriented differencing algorithms.
The authors identify difficult cases involving refactoring of mixed content, simultaneous moves and updates, and multiple attribute modifications on one node.
Quality evaluation relies partly on manually defined change clusters and a calibrated scoring function rather than a universally accepted XML-diff metric.
The approach provides pairwise change detection rather than persistent cross-version element identifiers or lineage spanning a long revision history.
The system does not address multimodal page regions, spreadsheet cells, or referring expressions from external messages.
raw_claims: JNDiff is intended to make XML differencing results resemble the changes that a human editor would expect to see.
The algorithm first identifies large matching portions of the two XML trees and subsequently refines the remaining differences.
Its refinement stages can represent operations such as updates and moves rather than reducing every modification to deletion followed by insertion.
The implementation is written in Java and was released as open-source software.
The document-quality experiment compares detected changes with manually identified or editor-tracked changes.
A synthetic evaluation corpus was built from 60 XML source documents covering formats including DocBook, Akoma Ntoso, IDML, XHTML, XSL-FO, and OpenXML.
The full experimental inputs and results were made available online by the authors.
Faxma is faster than JNDiff in the reported performance experiments.
The authors regard the extra computational cost as an acceptable tradeoff for more understandable text-centric change descriptions.
JNDiff is a pairwise XML differencer rather than a general provenance system for maintaining enduring identities across many revisions.

analyses.title: Schema-Less, Semantics-Based Change Detection for XML Documents
analyses.research_question: Can semantically corresponding XML elements be matched across successive versions without an external schema even when substantial structural reorganization makes conventional structural matching unreliable?
analyses.methodology: The paper derives semantic identifiers for XML element types directly from document instances, treating an identifier as an XPath-like description of information that distinguishes elements of the same type. A two-phase procedure first discovers identifiers based on descendant information and then augments unresolved cases with non-local information, with the identifier-computation cost bounded by O(n log n). For cross-version matching, the authors introduce a node-territory concept and require mutual evidence that each candidate node contains the identifying information of the other; a heuristic bypasses territory computation when a type's identifier is unchanged. The proposal is analyzed theoretically and illustrated through worked XML examples rather than through an implemented empirical benchmark.

key_findings.finding: Semantic identifiers can be inferred from an XML instance without requiring a DTD or XML Schema.
The proposed identifier-construction algorithm has a stated upper bound of O(n log n) for a document tree of size n.
The worked examples show that nodes retaining the same semantic information can be matched even when that information is reorganized into a substantially different XML structure.
key_findings.section: Section 5.2, Semantic Matching for Sample Documents

key_findings.finding: Naively attempting every cross-version node pairing is expensive, and the authors estimate whole-document matching at O(P*Q*(P log P + Q log Q)) before applying their heuristic.
When an element type retains the same identifier between versions, comparing evaluated identifier values directly can avoid the more expensive node-territory search.

The paper does not empirically establish real-world accuracy, robustness, or scalability relative to structural XML differencing systems because the proposed technique had not yet been implemented and benchmarked.

limitations: The central approach assumes that information identifying an element is generally conserved across revisions.
The paper provides worked examples and complexity analysis but no implemented-system benchmark or quantitative matching-accuracy evaluation.
For large documents, computing node territories is expected to consume a major share of processing time.
The matching heuristic relies on the expectation that identifiers for most element types remain unchanged between nearby versions.
No quantitative metric for semantic matching quality is evaluated.
The method concerns XML nodes rather than page regions, visual elements, spreadsheet cells, or message-to-document referring expressions.
The paper defines pairwise semantic identity but does not develop a persistent identifier namespace or lineage graph spanning an arbitrary revision history.
raw_claims: Structural XML differencing can fail when successive versions preserve information but reorganize the document structure substantially.
The paper treats semantic identity as distinct from identity based solely on tree structure.
An identifier describes information that distinguishes nodes belonging to a particular element type.
Identifiers may be local to an element's descendants or may require information outside that subtree.
Identifier discovery proceeds in two phases, beginning with local identifiers and then adding non-local identifying context.
The stated identifier-computation cost is bounded by O(n log n).
Two nodes are treated as semantically matching when the identifying information of each is admitted by the other's node territory.
Unmatched nodes after semantic matching are regarded as participants in a change.
Direct territory-based comparison of all possible node pairs can be computationally expensive.
The authors propose skipping territory computation when the semantic identifier for an element type remains unchanged.
The paper leaves implementation and empirical assessment as future work.

analyses.title: Rethinking Reading Order: Toward Generalizable Document Understanding with LLM-based Relation Modeling
analyses.research_question: Can LLM-inferred global reading-order relations provide a scalable structural prior that improves document understanding more broadly than conventional locally annotated reading-order supervision?
analyses.methodology: The authors prompt text-only and multimodal LLMs to infer directed reading-order relations among indexed document layout elements using their text, bounding boxes, and, for multimodal models, page imagery. For lightweight layout models, the inferred local and global relations are injected into attention through relation masks with learnable weighting, while generative QA models receive serialized reading-order relations in their prompts. Evaluation covers reading-order prediction, semantic entity recognition, entity linking, and document question answering on ROOR, EC-FUNSD, CORD, DocVQA, and InfoVQA, using LayoutLMv3, GeoLayoutLM, GPT-4o, and several other LLMs. Reported metrics include F1, ANLS, and exact match, together with ablations and computational-cost measurements.

key_findings.finding: LLM-generated reading-order relations align much less closely with adjacency-oriented human labels than a supervised LayoutLMv3 reading-order predictor, yet they can provide more useful global structure for downstream tasks.

On segment-level reading-order prediction, LayoutLMv3-large reports F1 80.49 whereas GPT-4o text-only reports 30.25, illustrating that the LLM-derived relations differ substantially from the benchmark's human-annotated relation convention.
Adding GPT-inferred reading order improves the reported EC-FUNSD SER and entity-linking scores for both LayoutLMv3-large and GeoLayoutLM compared with their respective baselines.
For GPT-4o document QA, adding inferred reading order raises DocVQA ANLS to 92.77 and InfoVQA ANLS to 77.15, with corresponding gains in exact match in the detailed ablation.

The authors report that generating reading-order relations for 6,000 pages requires 0.7 GPU-hours versus an estimated 25 hours of human annotation, and cached relation integration adds less than 0.5 ms per instance with under 1% parameter overhead.
Reading-order augmentation is not uniformly beneficial under every model, annotation source, and attention configuration; some ablation configurations exhibit small regressions.

The method models structural relations inside a document instance but does not provide cross-version region identity, revised-attachment lineage, or provenance links from an answer back through document versions.

limitations: Text-only LLM relation inference is sensitive to OCR errors.
Long-range and multi-page reasoning is limited by available computational resources and context length.
The generated relations depend on proprietary or large LLM behavior and prompting.
The paper states that code and derived data will be released only after corporate review rather than providing them with the paper.
The approach represents reading-order relations, not stable element identities across revised versions.
It does not address message-to-attachment reference resolution or explicit answer-to-source provenance chains.
Reading order is only one class of document relation and does not by itself establish semantic equivalence of elements across document revisions.
raw_claims: Conventional reading-order annotations are largely local and adjacency-oriented.
The proposed approach asks LLMs to infer broader relations among layout elements without supervised reading-order labels.
LLM-produced relations can disagree strongly with annotated reading-order links while still helping downstream document understanding.
Reading-order signals are injected into lightweight document models through relation-aware attention masks.
For generative question answering, inferred relations are serialized into textual relation descriptions.
The evaluation spans semantic entity recognition, entity linking, and document question answering.
GPT-inferred relations improve several LayoutLMv3 and GeoLayoutLM results on EC-FUNSD and CORD.
Adding reading-order information produces modest improvements on the reported DocVQA and InfoVQA results.
The authors report substantially lower relation-generation labor than manual annotation for a 6,000-page workload.
The paper promises future public release of code and derived data after corporate review.
The framework does not attempt to track the same layout element across successive revisions of a document.

analyses.title: Robust Table Detection and Structure Recognition from Heterogeneous Document Images
analyses.research_question: Can a unified visual pipeline robustly detect tables and recover their row, column, and spanning-cell structure across heterogeneous, distorted, curved, and sparsely ruled document images?
analyses.methodology: RobusTabNet first detects table regions using a CornerNet-style proposal mechanism that predicts opposing corners and exhaustively groups them, followed by Fast R-CNN classification and box refinement. Its table-structure recognizer uses a split-and-merge strategy: spatial CNN modules predict long-range row and column separator masks, geometric post-processing converts those masks into a cell grid, and a Grid CNN decides which adjacent grid cells should be merged into spanning cells. The models use lightweight ResNet-18/FPN components and are evaluated on public table-detection and structure datasets including cTDaR, PubLayNet, IIIT-AR-13K, SciTSR, and PubTabNet, as well as an in-house dataset containing challenging distorted and curved tables. Evaluation reports detection AP, precision, recall, F1, weighted-average F1, and TEDS-Struct, together with component ablations.

key_findings.finding: The CornerNet-plus-Fast-R-CNN detector achieves a weighted-average F1 of 94.9% on cTDaR TrackA, exceeding the comparison methods reported in the table.
On PubLayNet, the ResNet-18 detector reports AP 97.0 over IoU 0.5:0.95 and AP 92.0 at IoU 0.95, indicating particularly accurate localization at strict overlap thresholds.
The structure recognizer reports F1 99.3% on SciTSR and 98.7% on the more complicated SciTSR-COMP subset.
On PubTabNet, the method reports a TEDS-Struct score of 97.0%, above the listed comparison systems.
On the authors' distorted and curved in-house data, weighted-average F1 rises from 63.8% for SPLERGE to 94.6% for the proposed recognizer.
The Grid CNN cell-merging component raises weighted-average F1 from 90.9% without merging to 94.6%, and exceeds the tested relation-network and GCN alternatives.
The system recognizes geometry and cell structure within individual images but provides no mechanism for associating a detected table or cell with its counterpart in a later revision.

limitations: Nearby tables can be difficult to separate reliably.
Multi-line cell content can make separation-line estimation difficult.
Extremely dense tables can fail when masks for adjacent separation lines overlap.
The authors note that available datasets are dominated by black text on white backgrounds, leaving generalization to different backgrounds, fonts, and line colors insufficiently tested.
The challenging distorted-table evaluation uses an in-house dataset whose public availability is not established in the paper.
The method extracts table structure but does not assign durable cross-version table, row, column, or cell identifiers.
No document-revision provenance model or message-to-table reference-resolution mechanism is included.
raw_claims: RobusTabNet separates table processing into table detection and table structure recognition.
The detector generates table proposals from predicted corner pairs and then uses Fast R-CNN to reject or refine proposals.
The structure-recognition stage first splits a table into a grid and then merges grid cells when they belong to the same logical cell.
Spatial CNN propagation is used to capture long-range evidence for row and column separators.
Grid CNN performs visual reasoning over neighboring cells to recover spanning-cell structure.
The method is evaluated on several public benchmarks for both table detection and table structure recognition.
The reported SciTSR F1 is 99.3%, while the complicated subset score is 98.7%.
The reported PubTabNet TEDS-Struct score is 97.0%.
Experiments on an in-house dataset show a large advantage over SPLERGE for distorted and curved tables.
The authors identify very dense tables as a remaining failure mode because separator masks can overlap.
The system does not address longitudinal matching of cells or regions after a document is revised.

analyses.title: Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance
analyses.research_question: How can data provenance be formally separated into explanations of why an output exists and locations showing where an output value originated, and under what query restrictions are those notions preserved by query rewriting?
analyses.methodology: The paper develops a formal provenance framework over a deterministic semistructured data model in which every source location can be identified by a path from the root. It defines a deterministic query language, a rewrite system with a strongly normalizing normal form, and syntactic constructions for computing why-provenance through witness bases and where-provenance through derivation bases. The authors prove soundness, completeness, and rewriting-invariance results for selected query classes, including stronger invariance of minimal witness bases for equality-based queries and preservation of where-provenance for the restricted class of traceable queries. The work is theoretical and uses formal definitions, examples, lemmas, propositions, and proofs rather than an empirical dataset or implementation benchmark.

key_findings.finding: Why-provenance and where-provenance capture different questions: the former identifies source information sufficient to justify an output's existence, while the latter identifies source locations from which particular output values originate.
key_findings.section: Sections 1 and 4, Two Meanings of Provenance

key_findings.finding: The deterministic semistructured model gives every data item a location describable by a unique path, providing an explicit foundation for where-provenance.
The paper's query rewrite system is strongly normalizing, so every well-formed query can be transformed to the specified normal form after finitely many rewrite steps.
The Why procedure is proved sound and complete for computing the witness basis of a singular output value from a normal-form query.
For well-formed queries containing only equality conditions, the minimal witness basis is invariant across equivalent queries, with an extension indicated for certain inequality subclasses.
Where-provenance is not generally invariant under arbitrary equivalent query formulations, so the authors restrict their positive preservation result to traceable queries and their rewrite system.
For traceable queries, the derivation basis used as where-provenance is preserved when a query is rewritten by the paper's rewrite system.

The framework does not itself solve cross-version document-element identity; it traces query outputs to source locations within a database instance rather than matching evolving locations across revised source versions.

limitations: The query language and formal results require well-formed and well-defined queries and impose restrictions on variable bindings and query structure.
The deterministic query language is less expressive than general XML-QL, excluding features such as Kleene-star path patterns and supporting only hierarchical structures.
Where-provenance is not invariant for unrestricted equivalent queries.
The positive where-provenance rewriting result applies only to the restricted traceable-query class.
The authors leave a semantic characterization of where-provenance unresolved.
Necessary and sufficient conditions for the relevant well-defined query class remain future work.
The analysis is theoretical and supplies neither executable code nor an empirical provenance benchmark.
The framework identifies provenance locations inside source data but does not specify stable identities for locations as the underlying document or workbook changes across versions.
It does not model page regions, visual objects, spreadsheet-specific coordinates, external referring expressions, or hierarchical version-to-answer evidence identifiers.
raw_claims: The paper separates provenance into the question of why a result exists and the question of where a returned value came from.
Where-provenance requires an explicit way to identify source locations.
In the deterministic data model, a node is uniquely located by the path of edge labels from the root.
The proposed query language can express positive relational SPJU queries and positive nested relational algebra but is intentionally restricted.
Every well-formed query can be transformed into the paper's normal form by its strongly normalizing rewrite system.
A witness basis records source structures that validate the existence of an output value.
The paper gives an algorithm that computes witness bases and proves it sound and complete for normal-form queries.
Minimal witness bases are invariant across the specified class of equivalent equality-based queries.
Witnesses can be propagated through materialized views by composing provenance through nested queries.
Where-provenance is represented through a derivation basis that follows output variables back to source paths.
Equivalent general queries can have problematic or ambiguous where-provenance under a purely syntactic interpretation.
Restricting attention to traceable queries allows the derivation basis to be preserved under the paper's rewrite rules.
The provenance framework does not define persistent identities for source locations across independently revised versions.
